## 1. Quadratic hinge optimization

The inner ball in F makes the quadratic hinge coercive. For distinct
parameters, both affine functions are positive on a common neighborhood
of the marked point, and their difference is nonzero off a hyperplane;
integrated strict square convexity proves unique attainment. The C1
positive-part square permits direct differentiation. Stationarity gives
integral (z-x)h=0 and therefore integral h=integral h^2=B>0.

The claimed minimum-L2 density is exactly h/B. For any feasible density
rho, the affine mean identity gives 1=integral (1+a.(z-x))rho <=
integral h rho <=sqrt(B integral rho^2). Equality forces proportionality
to h and normalization fixes the factor 1/B. This proves actual primal
attainment and uniqueness, including cases where h vanishes on a
positive part of the facet. No positivity assumption on arbitrary rho
or absent infinite-dimensional duality is used. The point-facet case
is separately correct with counting measure.

## 2. Infinite prism and exact coefficients

At the fixed height-one mark, normal parameter v>=0 gives infinite
hinge integral, also when v=0 because an open tangential neighborhood
has positive affine intercept. For v=-b<0, direct vertical integration
is (1+b)^2/(2b) times the quadratic hinge with tangential parameter
u/(1+b). The factor is at least two, uniquely at b=1. Thus the unique
prism parameter is (2a_F,-1).

The actual convex cap under height 2h has volume 2 integral h=2B,
tangential mean x, and normal first moment 2 integral h^2=2B. Its
indicator certifies the value, and the normalized hinge bounds every
finite-mass feasible density with finite first moments. The distinction
between the convex cap and the displayed height region's extra bottom
points is measure-null and correctly stated.

## 3. Actual-body convergence and optimizer compactness

The geometric dependency supplies a fixed ball about (x,1) inside all
small-delta dilated bodies and a fixed compact tangential projection D.
The first fact supplies uniform hinge coercivity. The actual test
(0,-1) integrates to at most 2|D|. Hence the optimizing parameters are
bounded; this does not assume a compact parameter domain a priori.

At every fixed positive height, interior points of F eventually belong
to each section by the cone inclusion from F to one fixed interior
point of K. Outside F, membership eventually fails by compactness.
F's boundary is null. This proves the required local a.e. indicators.
Fatou applied to the actual optimizers gives a prism lower bound; the
uniform value upper bound excludes every limiting v>=0. The fixed
prism optimizer is a legal hinge parameter on every actual body and
has uniformly bounded positive-height support. Thus dominated
convergence gives the matching upper bound. Every cluster point is
the unique prism minimizer, proving convergence of the entire parameter
sequence. The argument never swaps an infimum with a limit.

## 4. Cap laws and all boundary cases

Convergence v_delta->-1 confines the actual optimal caps to a common
bounded cylinder. On that cylinder both their body indicators and cut
indicators converge a.e.; the exceptional set is contained in the
vertical facet boundary and one affine hyperplane, both null. Hence
symmetric-difference volume, normalized probability density, and first
moments converge. Integrating out the bounded height gives h/B, with
conditional mean h and overall normal mean one. Returning from the
dilation indeed produces the claimed weak law on the actual facet.

This works for nonsmooth F and K and closed caps. For d=1 the tangent
space is zero-dimensional and the cap length is exactly 2 delta for
small delta, agreeing with B=1. No untracked ambient/lattice affine
change occurs: this is an ordinary continuous-body normal dilation.

## 5. Exact calibration

For F=[0,1] and 0<x<=1/3, the stated affine positive part is
h(z)=3/2-z/(2x) on [0,3x] and zero afterwards. Direct integration gives
integral h=integral h^2=9x/4 and its centroid x. Thus 2B=9x/2. The
previously proved energy facet coefficient gives ratio 3(1-x), with
the normal limit at fixed x correctly distinguished from a uniform
edge limit.
